name: for  —  over a list
desc: Walks through a collection one item at a time. The variable after for is a name you choose.

name: range()
desc: Produces a run of numbers. The stop value is NEVER included — range(5) gives 0 to 4.
code:
for i in range(5):
    print(i, end=" ")
print()

for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i, end=" ")
print()

for i in range(0, 20, 5):      # start, stop, step
    print(i, end=" ")

name: for with an index
desc: range(len(...)) gives you the positions, which you need when you want the position as well as the value.

name: while
desc: Repeats while a condition stays True. YOU have to change something inside, or it never stops.
code:
count = 1
while count <= 5:
    print(count, end=" ")
    count = count + 1

name: break
desc: Leaves the loop immediately, no matter how many items are left.

name: continue
desc: Skips the rest of THIS turn and jumps to the next one. The loop keeps going.

name: Nested loops
desc: A loop inside a loop. The inner one runs completely for every single turn of the outer one.

name: Making one, and reaching in
desc: Ordered, changeable, and allows duplicates. Counting starts at 0; -1 is the last one.
code:
marks = [45, 72, 88, 61, 95]

print(marks)
print(marks[0])
print(marks[-1])
print(len(marks))

name: Slicing
desc: Take a range of items. The stop is not included, so [1:4] gives positions 1, 2 and 3.
code:
marks = [45, 72, 88, 61, 95]

print(marks[1:4])
print(marks[:3])
print(marks[2:])
print(marks[-2:])
print(marks[::2])
print(marks[::-1])     # reversed

name: Changing a list
desc: Unlike a string, a list can be edited in place.
code:
marks = [45, 72, 88]
marks[0] = 50
print(marks)

name: append / insert / extend
desc: append adds one to the end, insert puts one at a position, extend adds a whole list.
code:
m = [45, 72]
m.append(88)
print(m)
m.insert(1, 60)
print(m)
m.extend([91, 33])
print(m)

name: remove / pop / clear
desc: remove deletes by VALUE, pop deletes by POSITION and hands it back, clear empties the list.
code:
m = [45, 72, 88, 61]
m.remove(72)
print(m)
taken = m.pop(0)
print("popped", taken, "->", m)
print(m.pop())      # no number = the last one

name: sort / reverse / count / index
desc: sort changes the list itself. sorted() leaves it alone and hands back a new one.
code:
m = [45, 72, 88, 61, 72]
m.sort()
print(m)
m.sort(reverse=True)
print(m)
print("how many 72s:", m.count(72))
print("where is 88:", m.index(88))

name: sum / max / min on a list
desc: The three you will use constantly once real data arrives.
code:
marks = [45, 72, 88, 61, 95]
print("total  ", sum(marks))
print("highest", max(marks))
print("lowest ", min(marks))
print("average", sum(marks) / len(marks))

name: A tuple is a list that cannot change
desc: Round brackets instead of square. Everything about reading it is the same; writing is forbidden.
code:
point = (10, 20, 30)
print(point)
print(point[0])
print(point[1:])
print(len(point))

name: Trying to change one
desc: This is the whole difference, and the error names it: tuples do not support assignment.
out: TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment

name: Why use one at all
desc: When the values must not be edited by accident — fixed settings, coordinates, a database row.
code:
WEEKDAYS = ("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri")
print(len(WEEKDAYS), "working days")
print("Wed" in WEEKDAYS)
print(WEEKDAYS.count("Mon"), WEEKDAYS.index("Thu"))

name: A set throws away duplicates
desc: Curly brackets. No duplicates, and NO ORDER — so you cannot ask for set[0], and printing one gives the items in whatever order Python feels like. Wrap it in sorted() when you need a fixed order.
code:
depts = {"HR", "Tech", "HR", "Sales", "Tech"}

print(len(depts))          # the 2 repeats are gone
print(sorted(depts))      # sorted, so it looks the same every run
print("HR" in depts)

name: De-duplicating a list
desc: The most common real use: wrap a list in set() to see the distinct values.
code:
entries = ["HR", "Tech", "HR", "Sales", "Tech", "HR"]

print(sorted(set(entries)))
print("distinct departments:", len(set(entries)))

name: add / remove / discard
desc: remove complains if the item is not there. discard does not.
code:
s = {"HR", "Tech"}
s.add("Sales")
print(s == {"HR", "Tech", "Sales"})
s.discard("Finance")     # not there, no error
s.remove("HR")
print(sorted(s))

name: union / intersection / difference
desc: The school set theory, as code. Useful for comparing two groups of anything.

name: Key and value
desc: Instead of a position you use a name. That name is the key, and it has to be unique.
code:
emp = {"name": "Rahul", "dept": "HR", "salary": 47764}

print(emp)
print(emp["name"])
print(len(emp))

name: get()  —  the safe way to read
desc: Square brackets raise an error if the key is missing. get() hands back None, or whatever you choose.
code:
emp = {"name": "Rahul", "dept": "HR"}

print(emp.get("dept"))
print(emp.get("city"))                 # None, not an error
print(emp.get("city", "not recorded"))

name: Adding and changing
desc: Assign to a key that exists and it updates. Assign to a new one and it is added.
code:
emp = {"name": "Rahul", "dept": "HR"}
emp["salary"] = 47764      # new
emp["dept"]   = "Tech"     # changed
print(emp)
del emp["dept"]
print(emp)

name: keys / values / items
desc: The three views, and items() is the one you loop over when you want both halves.

name: Counting with a dictionary
desc: The pattern worth memorising: a dictionary of counts, built in one pass over the data.
